incidents.organisation: AusNet Services / AEMO (Victorian transmission and distribution networks)
incidents.consequences: Per Victorian Network Outage Review: over 1 million customers lost power across the event, over 531,000 off supply at the peak; six transmission towers collapsed and a 500 kV line failed; Loy Yang A generating units disconnected, requiring AEMO-directed load shedding; prolonged power outage payment supported more than 3,000 people still affected 7 days later. Per AEMO final report: generation impact 2,507 MW, customer load impact 325 MW shed. Per Energy Magazine (contemporary): about 90,000 customers lost power through AEMO load shedding and were restored; 90 per cent of customers reconnected within 48 hours (minister, as quoted); geography Victoria-wide, Gippsland hardest hit.
incidents.confirmed_at_first_report: Energy Magazine first version (published 15 Feb 2024 on page): 530,000 customers affected, Loy Yang A shut down, Moorabool-Sydenham 500 kV line tripped, AEMO directed AusNet to shed load, approximately 90,000 customers lost power via load shedding and had been restored.
incidents.unconfirmed_at_first_report: Early report attributed the Loy Yang A trip to 'the collapsing of two transmission towers'; the official review later states six towers collapsed. AEMO said it was investigating cause; restoration time for all customers was unknown ('days or more than a week in extreme circumstances').

incidents.consequences: Entire Sydney Trains network halted from about 2:45pm on Wednesday 8 March 2023 after the Digital Train Radio System (DTRS) failed; trains progressively recommenced around 4pm (Sydney Trains CEO, per Guardian) with significant delays through the evening peak; ABC: stopped 'more than one hour'; thousands of peak-hour commuters stranded; services to Newcastle, Wollongong and Blue Mountains also affected (Guardian). TfNSW COO described the DTRS as the vital link to over 300 trains (ABC).
incidents.confirmed_at_first_report: Network-wide halt at 2:45pm, cause stated as failure of the digital radio system connecting train crew with signallers and the rail operations centre; trains halted for safety; services resuming around 4pm; investigation announced.
incidents.unconfirmed_at_first_report: Root cause of the DTRS failure. Sydney Trains CEO said it was not believed to be a cyber-attack or related to a weekend software update ('early advice').

incidents.consequences: On Wednesday 1 May 2024, in two periods, some Qantas Frequent Flyer app users were shown other customers' names, upcoming flight details, points balance and status. Qantas: no financial information shown, points could not be transferred, boarding passes not usable, not aware of anyone travelling on incorrect boarding passes; app fixed by Wednesday evening. Guardian reported 'potentially thousands' of customers (unquantified by Qantas on the page text I extracted). On 3 May Qantas told members the root cause was a technology issue with no evidence of a cyber incident (ABC: understood to be a caching issue).
incidents.confirmed_at_first_report: App showing other customers' booking details in two periods; Qantas investigating; 'no indication of a cyber security incident'; possibly related to recent system changes.
incidents.unconfirmed_at_first_report: Number of customers affected; root cause (later stated as a technology/caching issue); whether sensitive travel information was shown to others (Qantas said it would contact customers directly).
